name: Giuoco Piano — Deviation Drills (Expert)
description: Real mistakes expert-level players actually play in the Giuoco Piano — and how to refute them.

lines.name: After 4.b4?!
lines.description: 4.b4?! was played in 10.9% of 16,114 games at this level. Find the refutation.
lines.explanation: 4.b4 is the Evans Gambit idea: a pawn offered for speed. Here Black simply takes it and steps back — …Bxb4, c3 Be7 — keeps the pawn, then plays …Na5 to trade off White's best bishop and …d5 to take the center White paid for. Every exchange subtracts a little more of White's compensation, until the gambit is just a pawn down and Black holds the plan. If you play b4, the compensation has to ADD up before it gets traded away.

lines.name: After 4.Bxf7+?!
lines.description: 4.Bxf7+?! was played in 0.7% of 16,114 games at this level. Find the refutation.
lines.explanation: 4.Bxf7+ is hope chess: a bishop sacrificed on a check, with no second attacker ready to ADD to it. After …Kxf7, Nxe5+ …Nxe5, Qh5+ Kf8, Qxe5, every trade subtracts another White attacker until the attack is gone and the Black king is safe on f8. Black then takes the center with …d5 and develops with tempo against the exposed queen. White paid his best bishop for an attack that removed itself.

lines.name: After 4.Ng5?!
lines.description: 4.Ng5?! was played in 0.3% of 16,114 games at this level. Find the refutation.
lines.explanation: 4.Ng5 attacks f7 with one piece and nothing behind it. The knight has moved twice while no other White piece ADDs pressure — and Black doesn't even have to defend: …Qxg5 simply takes the knight, because once it left f3, nothing guards it. White subtracted a developed piece from his own position and handed Black a free piece. An attack only works when the pieces behind it add up.

lines.name: After 4.d4?!
lines.description: 4.d4?! was played in 4.2% of 16,114 games at this level. Find the refutation.
lines.explanation: 4.d4 breaks the center before c3 is there to support it. The push looks like it ADDs, but a pawn break with no backup subtracts in every trade: …Nxd4 and …exd4 leave White recapturing into Black's development, with the center open while his king is still in the middle. Black is handed the plan White wanted — fast development and pressure against e4. The supported break (c3 first, then d4) is the whole point of this opening.

lines.name: After 5.O-O?!
lines.description: 5.O-O?! was played in 7.7% of 2,925 games at this level. Find the refutation.
lines.explanation: 5.O-O looks safe, but it spends the tempo White needed to protect e4 and fight for d4. Black takes the pawn at once: …Nxe4, because trying to win it back runs into …d5, opening the c5-bishop's diagonal against f2 — now aimed at a king that just committed to g1. White does regain the pawn (dxe5), but pays for it with …Bb6, …Qh4, and a passive Qe1 just to hold f2. Black ends up developed, active, and aiming at the king White showed him.

lines.name: After 5.d3?!
lines.description: 5.d3?! was played in 35.7% of 2,925 games at this level. Find the refutation.
lines.explanation: 5.d3 loses nothing; it's the quiet Giuoco Pianissimo. What it gives up is White's one chance to ADD in the center: d4, played now while Black is still uncastled. Against d3 Black is handed a plan with no problems to solve — …d6, castle, …Bb6, …Be6 — every piece developed comfortably, and White's first-move advantage subtracted to zero. The lesson isn't "d3 is bad," it's what the position was offering before White chose quiet.

lines.name: After 5.Ng5?!
lines.description: 5.Ng5?! was played in 0.5% of 2,925 games at this level. Find the refutation.
lines.explanation: 5.Ng5 aims at f7 again, but this time Black is too developed for a one-piece attack: …O-O just removes the target. The knight's whole trip — g5, back to f3 after …h6 — costs White two tempi and ADDs nothing, and while it wanders Black strikes first with …d5 and takes the center. White showed his idea before he had the pieces to back it, and handed Black the central break.

lines.name: After 5.Qe2?!
lines.description: 5.Qe2?! was played in 1.0% of 2,925 games at this level. Find the refutation.
lines.explanation: 5.Qe2 protects e4 passively instead of fighting for the center, and it parks the queen on the f1-bishop's own square, subtracting a developing move. Black castles, stacks on the e-file with …Re8, reroutes the bishop with …Bf8, and meets even the Ng5 idea with …Re7 covering f7 — then breaks first with …d5. White spent his queen move watching the center; Black spent his moves taking it.

lines.name: After 6...Bb6?!
lines.description: 6...Bb6?! was played in 5.1% of 906 games at this level. Find the refutation.
lines.explanation: 6…Bb6 takes the bishop off the fight for the center in the exact position where White's pawn pair is ready to roll. With no check and no pressure on d4, White ADDs for free: d5 kicks the c6-knight to the passive e7 square, e5 kicks the other knight out to e4, and White castles behind a rolling center while Black's knights are tangled on squares they're about to be chased from. The retreat handed White the center expansion …Bb4+ exists to prevent.

lines.name: After 6...Be7?!
lines.description: 6...Be7?! was played in 0.4% of 906 games at this level. Find the refutation.
lines.explanation: 6…Be7 puts the bishop back on a passive square inside Black's own position — no check, no pressure, nothing ADDed. White uses the free move the same way as against …Bb6, but harder: d5 removes the c6-knight from the center and drives it to the rim (…Na5, later marooned on b7), White reroutes with Bd3 so the bishop can't even be traded, castles, and builds behind the d5 wedge. Black's own queenside pawns have to lunge (…b5, …b4) just to find his pieces squares, weakening themselves in the process.

lines.name: After 6...Nxd4?!
lines.description: 6...Nxd4?! was played in 0.2% of 906 games at this level. Find the refutation.
lines.explanation: 6…Nxd4 grabs a center pawn by trading away the knight that was pressuring White's center — and White's recapture, Nxd4, lands a knight on the perfect central square for free. Black has spent his best-placed piece, given up the …Bb4+ check, and still has no pawn in the center: the e-pawn is already gone. White castles, develops Nc3, Bd3, Nf3 with everything pointing at the middle, and Black is reduced to trying …d5 late, into a finished White setup.

lines.name: After 6...d5?!
lines.description: 6...d5?! was played in 0.2% of 906 games at this level. Find the refutation.
lines.explanation: 6…d5 tries to ADD in the center before Black has the development to support it. After exd5 the strike has traded away Black's own central presence, and the follow-up check …Bb4+ only develops White for him: Nc3 blocks while developing, …Nxd5 recaptures into White's setup, and …Bxc3, bxc3 trades Black's active bishop off. White castles, puts the rook on the opened e-file with Re1, and Black is left pushing …b5 on the wing while the center — the thing …d5 was played for — belongs to White.
